newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Tensions high after Aleman wins Nicaragua vote.
newsitem.headline: Tensions high after Aleman wins Nicaragua vote.

text.p: Right-winger Arnoldo Aleman on Tuesday consolidated his firm victory in Nicaragua's presidential elections, but tensions were high as his defeated Sandinista rivals strongly disputed the vote.

Sandinista candidate Daniel Ortega, who refused to recognise the official results, sent top campaign lieutenants on a damage-control mission to explain that his claims of "serious irregularities" were not an attempt to be disruptive.
With anger and disappointment growing among the militant Sandinista rank-and-file, party leaders said they were taking pains to ensure Ortega's protests did not stir violence.

In the northern province of Matagalpa, however, where the record of malpractice in Sunday's elections was worst, opposition parties insisted there was deliberate fraud, perpetrated by Aleman's victorious Liberal Alliance.

"We condemn and repudiate the blatant manipulation and electoral fraud which has been orchestrated jointly by the president of the Provincial Election Council (Alberto Blandon) and the Liberal Alliance to which he belongs," 22 of the 23 parties in the province said in a communique.

In Matagalpa, an area of heavy fighting in the war between the Marxist Sandinista government and U.S.-backed Contra rebels in the 1980s, opposition parties said observers uncovered 3,000 Sandinista votes hidden in a house.
They said Sandinista supporters also beat up a man found with votes cast for their party concealed in his car. The reports could not be confirmed.

In Managua eight small parties that fielded presidential candidates demanded a recount, echoing the view of the Sandinistas that votes cast at polling stations did not tally with voting reports sent back to electoral headquarters where the vote count was taking place.

In the latest preliminary official results with almost three quarters of the vote counted, Aleman was well ahead of Ortega, 48.85 percent to 38.64 percent. He was easily above the 45 percent threshold needed to avoid a runoff.
With tempers running high, Ortega's aides took steps to fend off outbreaks of unrest by Sandinistas who are well organised and, as former revolutionaries, prone to protest.
"I have explained (to supporters) to keep calm and don't be rash," Ortega's campaign chief Alvaro Fiallos told reporters.
"The most important thing at this moment and going forward is to maintain the governability of the country," he said.

Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, present as one of thousands of observers, sought to diffuse tensions, saying defeated parties had "a legitimate concern" about the results that was being attended by electoral authorities.

After meeting with Ortega and Aleman and the head of the Supreme Election Council, he said authorities had agreed to provide information to political parties to enable them to double-check the results.

"The general consensus among all of the observers ... is that the election didn't have any degree of fraud that would subvert the decision of the Nicaraguan people," he told a news conference on Tuesday.
Many Nicaraguans agreed with Carter and criticised Ortega's party for being bad losers.
Aleman, the burly right-wing ex-mayor of Managua fondly dubbed "Fatman," caused rapture among his followers for keeping the left-wing Sandinistas, who ruled from 1979-1990, out of power.

Besides the presidency, Aleman's Liberal Alliance looked set to win the lion's share of seats in the National Assembly -- though perhaps not a majority -- and a clutch of town halls across the country, including the capital Managua.
In a move welcomed by the Sandinistas, who resented Aleman's decision to claim victory when just a fraction of the vote had been counted, he kept a low profile Tuesday.
